items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] America gets a chatbot
items.content_html:
The federal government has a chatbot.

President Donald Trump launched america.gov on Tuesday, a new site that looks like ChatGPT or Claude with a prompt box to query the federal government. The underlying LLM draws its responses from official state sources.

“With america.gov, the federal government no longer stands in your way, and it stands only at your service, and that’s what we’re doing,” Trump said at the unveiling. “We’re simplifying it, we’re glamorizing it, we’re making it what it should be.”

Trump signed an executive order Tuesday establishing the site, and according to the executive order, it excludes tax filing services provided by the Internal Revenue Service as well as services provided by the intelligence community and the Defense Department.

The site features a prompt box under a welcome message that reads, “Hello, America” and “Whatever you need from government, start here.” Suggested prompts include “How do I register my new business?,” “How do I replace my Social Security card?,” and “How do I book a campsite in a national park?”

The idea is that citizens can simply ask the chatbot for answers instead of navigating digital government bureaucracy online. The site says by next year people will be able to use it to enroll in Medicare, apply for a passport, find a federal government job, and more. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

“You’ll now have one front door for every single question,” Trump said. “Everything will be answered easily and quickly.”

The National Design Studio, Trump’s government design office staffed by former DOGE staffers and headed by Airbnb cofounder and Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia, designed the website. Like other sites the the studio has worked on—Realfood.gov and TrumpRX.gov, for example—the chatbot site is designed with a consumer sheen, with information laid out like an Apple product page in graphics inside squares with rounded corners. America.gov represents the office’s most ambitious rollout yet.

In an introductory message on the homepage that says in part that the site “uses AI to get simple answers only from official government sources,” in-line images and symbols are used like glyphs, a trend called Nouveau Rebus. The symbols are interactive. Click an arrow icon and it turns into a U.S. flag. Tap a trio of federal government seals and it shuffles into different agencies.

For all its gloss, America.gov is powered by an LMM, and comes amid rising public adoption of and worries over AI, including in government. A recent move to automate U.S. Web Design System accessibility testing has experts concerned it will hurt progress in making federal sites more accessible.

The website’s frequently asked questions page notes that “AI can make mistakes, so check the sources included with each answer before making an important decision.” There’s a feedback button to report a problem.

The FAQ also says the site doesn’t provide campaign or party information and “answers are based on published government sources.” The chatbot correctly identifies former President Joe Biden as the winner of the 2020 election, for example, instead of parroting Trump’s false claims. Using official government sources is great in theory for getting accurate, neutral government information from the source, but since this administration deletes government sites and scrubs information it doesn’t like, it also raises concerns about the potential to manipulate it.

America.gov doesn’t require a login to use, and according to its privacy policy, the site claims it collects no personal information, tracks no analytics nor locations, and keeps no conversations. A Guardian investigation this summer found National Design Studio has run commercial visitor-tracking software on sites that didn’t meet federal privacy standards.

While the website represents an innovation in digital government services, it’s part of a wider AI boom that’s seeing chatbots stuffed everywhere, and part of a larger bet that prompt boxes and AI responses are increasingly the way people interface with information today.

Pew Research Center found the percentage of U.S. adults who use AI is up from a third to nearly half since 2024. Even still, 71% believe the increased use of AI will make their personal information less secure, while 40% believe AI will have a negative impact on society over the next 20 years compared to just 16% who believe it will be positive.

Bringing government services into the AI age is a tall order ripe with challenges, but a successful chatbot could prove what’s possible. The federal government’s newest website represents a major public-facing test.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Earth’s day isn’t exactly 24 hours. The reason may lie deep inside the planet
items.content_html: Scientists may have solved why the length of Earth’s day changes by a few milliseconds over decades. Subtle shifts in the inner core appear to tug on the mantle, revealing a surprisingly dynamic world thousands of kilometers beneath our feet.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] This suitcase-sized spacecraft could hear the universe before stars existed
items.content_html: CosmoCube will use the far side of the Moon as a shield from Earth’s radio noise to search for a faint signal from the universe before the first stars existed. The suitcase-sized satellite could reveal how the cosmic dark ages ended and how dark matter helped build the first galaxies.

items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Scientists have discovered a new tick-borne virus in China that causes flu-like illness and may account for previously unexplained cases of fever, fatigue, digestive problems, and low platelet counts. Most patients with ALTNV alone recovered, but coinfections with another dangerous tick-borne virus were linked to more serious complications.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] James Webb reveals why planet formation is a race against time
items.content_html: JWST has revealed that young planetary systems lose their planet-building gas through a changing mix of powerful jets, molecular winds, and radiation-driven outflows. As the disks age and their gas disappears, giant planets face a shrinking window to build massive atmospheres.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Is the universe infinite? The answer gets weird fast
items.content_html: Measurements of ancient light from the cosmic microwave background suggest that the universe is remarkably flat. But that does not prove it is infinite, because the observable cosmos could be only a small patch of a much larger curved universe. Space could even be flat while wrapping around on itself in exotic ways.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] One CRISPR treatment cut “bad” cholesterol in half for a full year
items.content_html: A single dose of an experimental CRISPR therapy cut LDL cholesterol and triglycerides by about half in patients with difficult-to-treat lipid disorders. The reductions were still present one year later, with the highest dose lowering LDL by 52.5% and triglycerides by 47.8%.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] New soil test could reveal how soil microbes help feed plants
items.content_html: Scientists have streamlined a method for measuring DNA-bound phosphorus in soil, making it cheaper and easier while preserving its accuracy. The technique could reveal how soil microbes help recycle phosphorus and ultimately support more sustainable fertilizer and nutrient management.

items.title: [EarthSky] A black hole jet is aimed at us … and it’s in our galaxy
items.content_html:
For the first time, scientists have discovered a microblazar, a black hole system in our own galaxy with a jet pointed at Earth. It lies about 12,000 light-years away.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

🔭 ✏️

🔭 ✏️

Ancient DNA shows that adults and children buried together in medieval Sweden were often not members of the same immediate family, suggesting that burial choices reflected more than biological kinship. The research also revealed early gender-based burial customs and uncovered the remarkable story of a young woman who may have completed a pilgrimage across Europe.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists say house cats could help unlock better cancer treatments for humans
items.content_html: Scientists have mapped the genetics of cat cancer on an unprecedented scale and found surprising similarities with tumors in humans. The findings could help bring precision cancer treatments to cats while also revealing new clues about how human cancers develop and respond to drugs.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] That fresh cleaning smell could be filling your home with nanoparticles
items.content_html: Researchers found that scented cleaners can react with ozone indoors to create billions or trillions of invisible nanoparticles that can penetrate deep into the lungs. The pollution forms within minutes and, in some cases, may produce an inhaled particle dose comparable to or greater than standing near heavy traffic.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists may have misread a 2-billion-year-old clue about Earth
items.content_html: Scientists have found that a famous 2-billion-year-old chemical signature, once thought to record a massive global change in Earth’s carbon cycle, may instead have been produced by local magma, hydrocarbons, and methane-eating microbes. The discovery raises new questions about what was really happening as oxygen transformed the young planet.

items.content_html: In 1872, New York’s devastating epizootic gave the ASPCA’s young founder a powerful moral argument for animal protection

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Two astronauts who flew farther than anyone before are taking new NASA roles
items.content_html: Artemis II astronauts Victor Glover and Reid Wiseman are transitioning to emeritus status at NASA after their historic journey around the Moon earlier this year. The pair will continue advising and mentoring NASA teams as preparations accelerate for Artemis III and future lunar missions. Their experience with Orion and deep-space operations could prove especially valuable as NASA works toward returning astronauts to the lunar surface.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Zepbound and Mounjaro may turn on the body’s calorie-burning brown fat
items.content_html:

Tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, activated calorie-burning brown fat in obese mice, revealing a potential metabolic effect beyond appetite suppression. If confirmed in humans, the finding could help explain the drug’s powerful benefits and inspire more comprehensive treatments for obesity and diabetes.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] REM sleep paradox: Dreaming may drain the brain’s energy even as fuel supply rises
items.content_html: Scientists discovered a surprising energy paradox in the brain during REM sleep, the stage most closely associated with dreaming. Blood supply to the brain begins increasing even before REM starts, but neurons’ immediately available energy, measured as ATP, then drops. The finding suggests that dreaming may require such intense internal processing that neurons consume energy faster than it can be replenished.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] CERN has begun disconnecting the Large Hadron Collider
items.content_html: CERN has started replacing some of the Large Hadron Collider’s most important magnets as part of its High-Luminosity upgrade. The new superconducting magnets will produce fields about 40% stronger, allowing particle beams to be squeezed more tightly before they collide. That should create far more collisions for the ATLAS and CMS experiments to analyze, giving physicists a much larger window into the fundamental workings of the universe.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal
items.content_html: Researchers have shown that exotic quantum particles called non-Abelian anyons can perform the full range of operations needed for universal quantum computing. Using 54 qubits on Quantinuum’s H2 processor, they combined braiding and fusion to unlock capabilities that braiding alone could not provide.
